questions.stem: What does the 'a in fn pick<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str do?

options.text: Makes a and b live until the end of main
Tells the compiler to keep the returned string alive
Names a region of code, and claims all three references are valid across it
Allocates the return value with a longer lifetime

questions.why:
'a is a name, not a duration and not an instruction. The signature claims that both inputs and the output are valid across one common region, and the compiler checks that claim at every call site.

B is the misconception the whole unit exists to remove. Nothing in a signature extends anything's life; the values live exactly as long as the caller's scopes say, whether this function exists or not. An annotation that is false gets you an error, never a longer-lived value.

questions.stem:
Does this compile?

rust
fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}

options.text: Yes — elision assigns the first parameter's lifetime to the output
No — E0106, the compiler cannot tell which input the output borrows from
No — you cannot return a reference from a function
Yes, but only if both arguments are string literals

questions.why:
Elision rule 2 only fires when there is exactly one input lifetime. There are two here, so no output lifetime is assigned and you get error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier.

A is the tempting answer and it is what several other languages would do. Rust deliberately refuses to guess: "the first one" would be silently wrong half the time, and the caller would only find out through a lifetime error somewhere far away.

questions.stem: fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str compiles with no annotations. Why?

options.text: Because &str is always 'static
Elision rule 2: one input lifetime, so it is assigned to the output
Because the function does not allocate
Because str is a primitive type

questions.why:
Rule 1 gives the single input reference its own parameter 'a. Rule 2 then sees exactly one input lifetime and assigns it to every elided output lifetime. The signature the compiler actually works with is fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str.

A is a common and dangerous confusion. &str is not 'static — string literals are, because they are baked into the binary, but a slice of a String lives exactly as long as that String.

questions.stem:
Which of these signatures need an explicit lifetime annotation? Choose all that apply.

rust
fn a(s: &str) -> usize
fn b(s: &str) -> &str
fn c(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str
fn d(&self, other: &str) -> &str          // returns a slice of `other`

options.text: a
b
c
d

questions.why:
a returns no reference, so nothing needs assigning. b has one input lifetime, so rule 2 handles it.

c has two, and neither rule 2 nor rule 3 applies — that is E0106.

d is the sneaky one. It compiles, because rule 3 assigns self's lifetime to the output. It is simply wrong: the body returns a slice of other, so you get E0621 instead. Elision succeeded and produced a signature you did not mean.

questions.stem:
Does this compile?

rust
struct Excerpt {
    part: &str,
}

options.text: Yes — the field borrows from whatever built the struct
No — E0106; a struct field gets no elision
Yes, but the struct can only hold literals
No — structs cannot contain references at all

questions.why:
All three elision rules are about fn signatures. A struct has no arguments, so there is nothing for the compiler to infer a lifetime from. You must declare one: struct Excerpt<'a> { part: &'a str }.

D is wrong and worth ruling out firmly. Structs holding references are the foundation of every zero-copy parser in Rust — the point of <'a> is to make them safe, not to forbid them.

options.text: The parser is allocated for the duration 'a
A Parser<'a> value may not outlive whatever it borrowed
The parser keeps its source string alive
The parser can only be used inside a block labelled 'a

questions.why:
The parameter is a constraint carried in the type, not a field and not storage. It says: this value contains a borrow, so it must die before the thing it borrowed from does.

C inverts the relationship, and that inversion is the heart of the confusion. Rust references never keep anything alive — that is reference counting, which is Rc and Arc. A borrow only constrains the borrower.

questions.stem:
Does this compile?

rust
fn greeting() -> &'static str {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    &s
}

options.text: Yes — 'static makes the string live for the whole program
No — E0515, you cannot return a reference to a local
Yes, because string literals are 'static
No — String cannot be borrowed as &str

questions.why:
s is dropped at the closing brace, so the returned reference would point at a dead frame. 'static is a well-formed claim that happens to be false, and the compiler checks claims.

A is exactly the misconception to shed: writing a lifetime does not create one. No annotation makes a local outlive its own function. The fix is always to return an owned value — here, -> String and String::from("hello").

options.text: Values of T live for the whole program
T contains no reference with a lifetime shorter than the program
T must be a constant or a literal
T is stored in static memory

questions.why:
It is a bound on the type, not a promise about any value. String, i32, Vec<u8> and &'static str all satisfy T: 'static, because none of them holds a short-lived borrow. A freshly allocated String dropped a line later satisfies it perfectly.

A is how nearly everyone reads it, and it is why thread::spawn's F: 'static sends people looking for Box::leak. The bound only means the value could be kept indefinitely, not that it will be.

questions.stem: Which of these types satisfy T: 'static? Choose all that apply.

options.text: String
&'static str
&'a str for some local 'a
Vec<u8>
Parser<'a> where 'a is a function-local region

questions.why:
A, B and D own their data or borrow only from the program's own binary, so nothing inside them can expire. C and E carry a short-lived borrow, which is exactly what the bound rules out.

The pattern: owning types are always 'static; borrowing types are 'static only when what they borrow is. This is why the fix for a stubborn 'static bound is so often "own the data" — String instead of &'a str.

questions.stem:
Does this compile?

rust
struct Parser<'a> { src: &'a str }

impl Parser {
    fn src(&self) -> &str { self.src }
}

options.text: Yes — the impl can elide the lifetime
No — E0726; the impl must name the type's lifetime parameter
No — methods cannot return references to fields
Yes, but only for &'static str

questions.why:
Parser is not a type; Parser<'a> is, for each 'a. An impl block has to say which one, exactly as it would for a generic type parameter: impl<'a> Parser<'a>.

The compiler suggests Parser<'_>, which silences this error and is often not what you want. '_ introduces a fresh anonymous lifetime, so you lose the ability to say "this method returns something valid for as long as the source", which is usually the whole reason the struct has a lifetime.

questions.stem:
Does this compile?

rust
let best;
{
    let joined = vec!["a", "bbb"].join("-");
    best = joined.split('-').max_by_key(|w| w.len()).unwrap();
}
println!("{best}");

options.text: Yes — best holds a copy of the word
No — E0597, joined does not live long enough
No — max_by_key returns an owned String
Yes, because &str is Copy

questions.why:
Every slice from split points into joined's heap buffer, which is freed at the closing brace. best is read after that.

D is the trap, and it is true but irrelevant. &str is Copy — copying it duplicates a pointer and a length, and both copies still point at the same dead buffer. Copying a reference never copies what it refers to. The fix is to move joined out to the outer scope, or to call .to_string().

questions.stem: What is the runtime cost of a lifetime annotation?

options.text: None — lifetimes are erased before code generation
One word per reference, to store the region
A check on every dereference
It depends on how many lifetime parameters the function has

questions.why:
Lifetimes exist only in the type checker. By the time the compiler emits machine code they are gone, and a &'a str is what it always was: a pointer and a length. Two functions differing only in their annotations compile to identical instructions.

That is why lifetimes can be strict without being expensive — the entire analysis is a compile-time proof, and a proof does not need to be carried around at runtime.

questions.stem: Why is &'long T accepted where &'short T is expected?

options.text: Covariance — a reference valid for longer is valid for shorter
The compiler shortens the referenced value's life to match
It is not accepted; the lifetimes must match exactly
Because &T is Copy

questions.why:
Lifetimes have a subtyping relation and &T is covariant in it: something valid across a big region is certainly valid across a smaller one contained in it. This is why most code never notices lifetimes have a subtyping relation at all.

B has the causation backwards. Nothing is shortened; the claim is weakened, which is always sound. Note that &mut T is invariant in T for the opposite reason: you can write through it, so substituting a shorter lifetime inside would let you store a dangling reference.

questions.stem: thread::spawn requires F: Send + 'static. What does that stop you doing?

options.text: Spawning more than one thread from a function
Capturing a reference to a local variable in the closure
Returning a value from the thread
Using String inside the thread

questions.why:
The spawned thread has no bound on when it finishes, so it may still be running after the spawning frame is gone. 'static forbids the closure's type from holding any borrow that could expire by then.

D is the answer people fear and it is wrong: String owns its buffer, so it satisfies 'static and move-ing one in is completely fine. If you genuinely need to borrow a local, std::thread::scope guarantees the threads finish first and lifts the bound.

questions.stem: A function signature needs three lifetime parameters and you cannot get it to compile. What is the most likely correct move?

options.text: Add 'static to every reference
Box the return value
Make the struct or function own its data instead of borrowing it
Add unsafe and transmute the lifetimes

questions.why:
Three lifetimes in one signature almost always means the data is shaped wrong. A struct of borrows that wanted to be a struct of values, or a returned view that wanted to be a returned String, produces exactly this kind of pile-up.

A does not work: 'static is a claim, and adding it to something that is not 'static moves the error rather than removing it. D compiles and is how you get use-after-free back. The annotation was faithfully describing a constraint — the real decision is whether you wanted the constraint.
